content:
You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- Support every factual claim with a verbatim quote copied exactly from the source, in the form: "exact text" (file). Never paraphrase inside the quotation marks. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no citation.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a
  <verification> message, you are in revision mode: fix ONLY the flagged problems by calling
  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.
  Keep everything else unchanged, and reply "Done" when finished.
  Never call edit_draft before you have given an answer.

Discuss the similarities and differences between a simple installment loan and a mortgage. Explain in what situations one option should be chosen over the other. Limit the discussion to 250 words.

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

name: read
content:
1	Installment Loans
     2	 A loan is something that is borrowed. In the case where this is a sum of money the amount that will
     3	be paid by the borrower will include the original amount plus interest.
     4	
     5	
     6	 Some loans require full payment on the maturity date of the loan. The maturity date is when all
     7	principal and/or interest must be repaid to the the lender. Consider a one year loan of $1000 at a
     8	simple interest rate of 5%. At the end of one year (the maturity date) the borrower will pay back
     9	the original $1000 plus the interest of $50 for a total of $1050.
    10	
    11	
    12	 For major purchases such as vehicles or furniture there is a different type of loan, called the
    13	installment loan. The average consumer cannot afford to pay $25000 or more for a new vehicle and
    14	they may not want to wait three or four years until they have saved enough money to do so. The
    15	qualifying consumer has the option of paying for the item with an installment loan.
    16	
    17	
    18	 Installment loans do not require full repayment of the loan on a specific date. With an installment
    19	loan the borrower is required to make regular (installment) payments until the loan is paid off.
    20	Each installment payment will include an interest charge. An installment loan can vary in length
    21	from a few years to perhaps twenty years or more (in the case of real estate).
    22	
    23	
    24	 Consider an installment loan for a $4000 television. The purchaser takes out a $4000 loan with a
    25	four-year term at an interest rate of 4.5%. The monthly installment payments will be $91.21.
    26	Although the television has a purchase price of $4000, the total cost to the purchaser will be more
    27	than $4000. The total of the installment payments will be:
    28	
    29	
    30	 Total Installment Payments = Number of Installment Payments x Payment Amount =
    31	
    32	
    33	 4 years x 12 payments/year x $91.21/mth = $4378.08
    34	
    35	
    36	 The $4000 television ends up costing $4378.08 because the consumer is charged interest. Each
    37	payment includes an interest component that adds to the overall cost of the item. The total of the
    38	interest charges is referred to as the finance charge on the loan.
    39	
    40	
    41	 Finance Charge
    42	
    43	
    44	 The finance charge is the sum of the interest charges on a loan. These interest charges are
    45	embedded in the installment payments. To calculate the finance charge:
    46	
    47	
    48	 Finance Charge = Total Installment Payments – Loan Amount
    49	
    50	
    51	 = (Number of Installment Payments x Payment Amount) – Loan Amount
    52	
    53	
    54	 For the $4000 television the finance charge will be calculated as follows:
    55	
    56	
    57	 Finance charge = Total Installment Payments – Loan Amount =
    58	
    59	
    60	 (4 years x 12 payments/year x $91.21/payment) – $4000 = $4378.08 – $4000 = $378.08
    61	
    62	
    63	 Over the 4-year term of the loan the purchaser will have paid the $4000 loan amount plus an
    64	additional $378.08 in interest (the finance charge).
    65	
    66	
    67	 Sometimes the borrower will make an initial payment at the time of purchase. This is called a down
    68	payment. When a down payment is made the remaining amount is the amount financed or the loan amount.
    69	
    70	
    71	 Amount Financed
    72	
    73	
    74	 The amount financed or loan amount is the purchase price of the item less any down payment:
    75	
    76	
    77	 Amount Financed = Purchase Price – Down Payment
    78	
    79	
    80	 Consider the $4000 television. Assume the purchaser makes a down payment of $1500.
    81	
    82	
    83	 The amount financed is: Purchase Price – Down Payment = $4000 – $1500 = $2500.
    84	
    85	
    86	 In this case the purchaser borrows $2500 rather than $4000. The amount financed is therefore $2500.
    87	Assuming the same 4-year term and an interest rate of 4.5%, the installment payments on the $2500
    88	will be reduced to $57.01 per month. In this case the finance charge will be calculated as follows:
    89	
    90	
    91	 Finance charge = Total Installment Payments – Loan Amount =
    92	
    93	
    94	 (4 years x 12 payments/year x $57.01/payment) – $2500 = $2736.48 – $2500 = $236.48
    95	
    96	
    97	 With the down payment of $2500 the total finance charges will be reduced to $236.48 from $378.08.
    98	
    99	
   100	 The total cost of the television to the purchaser will be:
   101	
   102	
   103	 Purchase Price + Finance Charge
   104	
   105	
   106	 = $4000 + $236.48 = $4236.48
   107	
   108	
   109	 Alternatively we can calculate:
   110	
   111	
   112	 Total Installment Payment + Down Payment
   113	
   114	
   115	 = $2736.48 + $1500 = $4236.48
   116	
   117	
   118	 As one can see, the finance charges are a hidden but added cost. This cost will become more
   119	pronounced with more expensive purchases such as with real estate.
   120	
   121	
   122	 Loan Payments
   123	 When consumers obtain installment loans they often just trust the lender to determine the
   124	installment (periodic) loan payments. In Example1 Paul purchased a home entertainment system at a
   125	total cost of $6000. He obtained a three year loan at an interest rate of 7.5%. If Paul attempts to
   126	calculate his monthly payment by simply dividing the loan amount by the number of payments he will
   127	underestimate his monthly payment as he has ignored the interest component:
   128	 $6000 ÷ 36 = $166.67
   129	 Paul’s actual monthly payment of $186.64 is slightly higher than Paul’s estimate because of the
   130	interest component.
   131	 The actual amount of a periodic loan payment can be determined using a formula, a table or
   132	technology. In this section we will illustrate the use of a formula.
   133	
   134	
   135	 Amortization
   136	 Amortization is the process of spreading out a loan into a series of fixed payments. A portion of
   137	each payment will be applied to the interest charge and a portion will be applied to the principal
   138	amount of the loan. Although each payment is equal, the amount that applies to the interest versus
   139	the prinipal will change with each payment period. We can get a better sense of the impact that a
   140	loan payment has by examining the amortization schedule for a loan.
   141	 Consider the amortization table for the installment loan in Example 5. Recall that the loan amount
   142	is $5000 at 6% for 5 years and annual payments are $1186.98. Note then that for each year the sum of
   143	the interest and principal is equivalent to the payment of $1186.98. Refer to Figure 1 for the
   144	amortization schedule of this loan.
   145	
   146	
   147	 Mortgages
   148	 A long term loan that is used for the purchase of a house is called a mortgage. It is called a
   149	mortgage because the lending agency requires that the house be used as collateral for the loan. This
   150	means that if the mortgage holder is unable to make the payments the lender can take possession of
   151	the house.
   152	
   153	
   154	 Mortgages generally tend to be for longer time periods than an installment loan and the terms of
   155	the mortgage will often change over the course of the mortgage. Take for example the purchase of a
   156	house with a twenty year mortgage. The purchaser might sign a mortgage agreement for a five year
   157	term. The mortgage agreement will include the interest rate, the frequency of payments and
   158	additional rules which may allow the mortgage holder to make lump sum payments or change the payment
   159	amount. At the end of the five year term a new agreement will be required and the conditions of the
   160	mortgage usually change.
   161	
   162

163	 Although it is possible to do the calculations manually, that is beyond the scope of this book. We
   164	will use technology to calculate the periodic payments and interest charges and to generate an
   165	amortization schedule.
   166	
   167	
   168	 Example 8 will illustrate that amortizing a mortgage is similar to amortizing other loans except
   169	that the mortgage amortization generally involves many more payment periods.

**Similarities:** Both are loans repaid with the original amount plus interest, through regular payments: "the borrower is required to make regular (installment) payments until the loan is paid off" (doc.txt), and mortgage amortization is "similar to amortizing other loans" (doc.txt). Both can be long-term: an installment loan "can vary in length from a few years to perhaps twenty years or more (in the case of real estate)" (doc.txt).

**Differences:** A mortgage is "a long term loan that is used for the purchase of a house" (doc.txt), while installment loans serve "major purchases such as vehicles or furniture" (doc.txt). A mortgage requires the house as collateral: "if the mortgage holder is unable to make the payments the lender can take possession of the house" (doc.txt). Mortgages "generally tend to be for longer time periods than an installment loan" (doc.txt), and "the terms of the mortgage will often change over the course of the mortgage" (doc.txt): a twenty-year mortgage may be signed for a five-year term, after which "a new agreement will be required and the conditions of the mortgage usually change" (doc.txt). The agreement may allow "lump sum payments or change the payment amount" (doc.txt).

**When to choose which:** The document ties the choice to the purchase — an installment loan for vehicles or furniture, a mortgage for a house. It does not discuss other decision criteria.
